articles.title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build
articles.full_content:
Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying

[W]e should be more ambitious with the software we build

There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail, this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath, this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail, multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader, this money overflow bug, etc.

This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free, but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed.

That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post).

As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday, and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever.

But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use.

If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more.

Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were:

  • Ripgrep
  • Compiling Rust
  • Syscall and filesystem overhead

At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about, this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun" project where I wasn't trying to do the optimal thing), and a Rust that sped up builds for my projects (huge improvement for cold builds, moderate for warm, limited by wanting to avoid forking the Rust compiler front-end). For syscalls and filesystem overhead, just switching development from Mac to Linux improved this a lot, and of course this is another thing that can be sped up a lot as well, especially when agents are hammering lots of small filesystem operations (it's not uncommon to see my machine waiting on filesystem ops because the standard OS filesystem interface wasn't designed with modern disk performance in mind). With modern disks, there's no reason to use the *nix filesystem API. In the past, writing a developer toolchain that uses direct I/O instead of normal filessytem operations would've been an absurd endevaor, but that's totally doable now.

For someone like me who doesn't know anything about regexes, string matching algorithms, compilers, interpreters, etc., this set of projects would've taken a year or more to get to "works for me" quality. Instead, this was a low single-digit number of hours of my time. If I wanted to make any of these things meet a "useful product or open source project" quality bar, that would be a lot more work0, but it's still pretty incredible how much this process is sped up.

My read of Malis's meaning when he says “we should be more ambitious with the software we build”, is that it doesn't even occur to people to do these things that are now easy. For weeks, every time I logged into Twitter, I saw someone complain about how Rust compilation is slow and is limiting development velocity (I think this wasn't actually true when I saw the complaints, in that this was before 5.6 Sol and 6 Astra were available on Cerebras, and if you measured where the time actually went, Rust compilation time wasn't actually that much of a bottleneck at the time). Sure, Rust compliation is slow. You can just write a Rust interpreter as well as speed up compilation directly. There are problems like this which I see people complaining about daily that are solvable without a lot of time or effort now. As far as I can tell, these problems are problems because people are implicitly carrying around a pre-agentic cost model. Ten years ago, the kind of person who implemented a new compiler because their compiler was slow was the kind of person who started programming a new 3d game engine when they wanted to make an indie game, i.e., the kind of person who never ships anything. Most productive programmers I know still have an aversion to this kind of thing, even though it is now actually reasonable to implement this kind of thing now.

Another project I previously mentioned was this Azul AI which is superhuman at matched time controls. When I did that (with GPT-5.1/5.2), with zero AI knowledge, it took about 5 hours of my time to get something superhuman, and about 20 hours of my time to become what appeared to be the strongest AI at the time, including being stronger against humans than this AI that was used to cheat on Board Game Arena. Gabriel Cangussu recently built an AI that demolishes my AI, and AFAICT, it took him substantially less time than my AI took me. From talking to him about it, one key difference is that Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 have a much better understanding of board game AIs. When I used GPT-5.1/5.2, pretty much every suggestion they had was wrong and I had to do a lot of steering to get things to be remotely reasonable. If I had GPT read a codebase or a paper to implement relevant techniques from the paper, it would fail. If I read the paper myself and named a technique, it would say it did the technique, but it would generally do something that superficially looked like the technique but wasn't the actual technique until I issued some corrections. When the model is that far from being able to do the right thing, if you have no background in the area, it's fairly time consuming to check if the model did the right thing since you have to learn enough about what it's supposed to do to be able to check that it did what was claimed.

When I did that project, I said to friends that I didn't think the state models were in could last. It seemed impossible that they wouldn't get good enough to be able to read a paper and implement the techniques soon, and it seemed like they should also be able to pick out codebases and papers to crib from as well. From my experience messing around a bit with Fable 5 and Cangussu's experience with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, that seems to have happened, which is a huge time saver for someone like me who doesn't know anything about board game AIs (I know a little bit now, but still less than any real AI researcher).

For any particular domain, like board game AIs, you can say, "who cares? Board game AIs don't matter", but I've found this increase in capability to be true in quite a few different domains. Just for example, I did this toy eval of verification and test techniques with GPT-5.6 Sol implementing zstd on medium and xhigh. I haven't had time to write it up, but when I published that post, I also re-did the evals with GPT-6 Astra. 6 Astra was so good that I had to find different evals because models had advanced too much. For zstd, 6 Astra succeeds at passing all of the registered tests more than 99% of the time across all conditions, even the ones that significantly impair performance, like using TDD (and, BTW, it does it more cheaply as well, taking about $1 to implement zstd). I ended up using the IMAP RFC, which 5.6 Sol couldn't do effectively, and Pandoc, which is a pretty major thing to implement as it needs to be able to read and write many different formats.

BTW, when people have said they used the new model and everything just works, software is solved, etc., I haven't found this to be true at all. It's true that there are a lot more things the newer model can one-shot, where things basically just work, but this just means that I end up working on more ambitious things where models still struggle. I'm more productive and can work faster, but I find that, in terms of what I'm doing, I get farther from "it just works" with each more capable model because the gap between what the model can verify effectively without significant handholding and what the model can implement has been increasing. All of that is a long-winded and less eloquent way of saying: we should be more ambitious with the software we build.

Thanks to Laurence Tratt, Yossi Kreinin, Alex Kolovsky, and Michael Malis for comments/corrections/discussion.

I've had this note on my recent posts, which also applies to this one. In order to get more posts out, I'm trying to crank posts out in half an hour and not review them much. This definitely means less well-supported posts. If I were writing this in my standard style, I would've had comprehensive benchmarks for all of my projects that I mentioned. Instead, I did a quick comparison that satisfied my curiosity and am writing this up without rigorous benchmarking, and there are maybe twenty or thirty things in this post that I'd like to do but haven't done.

I haven't even written up this Rust interpreter. If, five years ago, I'd cobbled together a Rust interpreter that got a 50x speedup on cold compiles and 2x on warm/cached builds (with much more being possible if edits to the Rust compiler were in bounds), that woudl be a super interestin thing that I'd want to write up, but even operating in this mode where I barely edit posts and just blast them out, this isn't interesting enough to write up because it's so easy to do things that would've been considered very interesting not all that long ago.

Appendix: we should be less ambitious with the software we build

Here's a comment from Yossi Kreinin, quoted (with permission, of course):

If you publish this I will publish a response explaining that for most people they should be less ambitious with the software they build with AI or they'll experience abject failure. I think a lot of the problems don't lend themselves that well to "agentic loops" since you don't have clear pass/fail criteria, and even when you do most people have trouble reasoning about giant black boxes which they can impose constraints on but can't understand the innards of [I include myself in this set.] This is a little bit like microservices I guess, where some people both need it and are very good at using it but likely for most people, they need it less and can't use it well at all. I sort of envy the ones who should and actually can be this ambitious about the software they build of course; not saying you shouldn't be more ambitious at all but moderating said ambition is a big part of handling the current situation for most I think

I have a similar thought about "there's no reason for software to be slow" BTW; in many cases, if you use AI to speed up some flow, you will add a bunch of messy code that will be overfit for the use case you tested on and will neither generalize, perf-wise, for all the use cases you should care about, nor will be maintainable upon future changes. If you know what you're doing and you understand how the system should be decomposed into parts and when it makes sense to go all-in on optimizing some part or a combination of them working together and how to properly benchmark it, etc., then things are great, but if for instance you have a manager who thinks there's no reason for software to be slow and he pushes people to use AI to make random parts of the software fast... Run for cover

My feeling is that, overall, the situation here is a bit analogous to the discussion here about why I don't like when people talk about how AI gives a 100x or 1000x productivity increase. There are some things that are sped up by a very large factor, easily over 1000000x. And some things don't currently get sped up at all. If you do exactly what you would've done five years ago, but with AI, the speedup is fairly poor because of Amdahl's law. But, in the general case, you can choose what to speed up and if you're looking for things that are productive to do, this often seems to involve things that were previously too expensive to do.

And, I think that you can often set up systems that have some kind of self-checking property even when most people wouldn't. This discussion of the implementation of Guards of Atlantis 2 is an example of that. It's a poor choice for an AI project because the official rules are a mess of ambiguous and contradictory English text (it's probably the game I've seen humans misplay at the highest rate, and the rules are confusing enough that the designer has often changed their mind about what their own rules mean despite continually maintaining that the rules are perfectly clear and one can play the game by simply reading the rules as written). If you try to produce a working set of rules in a naive way, AI won't really help with this (although it can speed up implementation once you have a clean spec), but for that, I was able to set up some kind of janky set of consistency checks between all of the inconsistent explanations of the game rules, which got fairly close to a correct set of rules (approximately as close as what someone else did with much more human effort and less of a systematic approach), which was enough to compare it to someone else's implementation and get a working set of rules. This setup did cost a lot more in tokens than a more manual approach. But it was "only" a month or two of the $200/mo OpenAI subscription with GPT-5.1/5.2, which is a lower cost than the cost in time of me sitting down and writing a clean spec for the game, i.e., a copy of the rules that is actually consistent and correct.

I feel like a lot of problems are in something like this class of problem, where it's possible to set up some kind of at least partially self-checking setup that a human can spend a small amount of time on. This also feels analogous to the situation about software testing at large, where (before coding agents) I found fuzzing and property-based testing to be highly effective. For most domains, people told me some kind of reason this kind of testing wouldn't work, but when I've tried these techniques with all of the domains people told me these techniques don't work for, they work fine. They're somewhat more work to apply, but they're still applicable and, AFAICT, more efficient and effective than writing traditional unit tests.

Part of the gist of Yossi's comment is that people aren't doing this kind of thing. Considering how many more bugs I see now than I used to, e.g., the last time I opened up the web chat for a big AI lab, I ran into a double-digit number of bugs within one minute, it's hard to say that Yossi is wrong. But, to that point, I still have my original opinion. Just because other people are pumping out vast quantities of barely working slop doesn't mean that you have to do the same thing.

Appendix: a few "random" examples

The examples in the body of the post I gave for things I've done are tooling things I never would've done. There are a lot more things like that as well since it's so easy to build "works for me" quality tooling that's intended solely for me. I do think it's possible to go further than is productive, e.g., Steve Yegge wrote a lot about Gas Town and how productive it was, but when he was building his next agentic framework, he noted that he never used Gas Town to successfully build anything other than Gas Town, people were into Ralph Loops for a while even though, when I tried comparing them, they seemed worse than just doing the naive thing I was doing at the time, normal loops with context where you sometimes clear context as appropriate instead of doing it by default at the completely arbitrary point of when a single turn is completed, etc., so I've tried to stick to things where the impact is pretty direct. Besides the obvious reason this has been effective, the dramatic change in model and harness capability over time means that what tooling it makes sense to build changes very quickly, so spending a lot of time working on any particular tool that will be suboptimal at best and quite possibly obsolete in three months doesn't really make sense.

And, for a lot of my personal tools, my assumption is that an AI lab will obsolete anything I make in short order. For a very silly example of this, I have a tool that was useful since the release of GPT-5.6 Sol that restarts codex when it finds a memory leak. Presumably, OpenAI will fix this at some point and this tool will become worthless. For a slightly less silly example, take the Rust interpreter I had some agent build. For token-budget reasons, a lot of things that ought to be done for a very high-performance interpreter haven't been done.

For example, the interpreter doesn't modify the actual Rust front-end compiler to make it easy to take updates; performance would be much better if I just made changes to the Rust front-end, but I don't have the token budget to maintain a compatible fork of the Rust compiler, but this shouldn't be a problem for OpenAI. OpenAI spent $10B+ on getting access to Cerebras while also preventing Anthropic from having access.

Funnily enough, for coding, on many tasks, if you actually use one of their SOTA models and compare it to what you get from Anthropic, the actual speedup isn't all that large because of time spent on things like compiling Rust. Given that they were willing to commit $10B+ on this, it stands to reason that they'll eventually do a better job at speeding up the relevant tools than anyone could feasibly do outside an AI lab, so there's not much point in spending too much effort on this (this could arguably be untrue if non-coding tasks are expected to completely dominate future OpenAI revenue in the short term, but even then, given what they pay for tokens vs. what I pay, it still seems like it would make sense for them to speed a lot of these things up given that I could do it outside of a lab; perhaps there's some kind of argument like, if you have access to their usage data, there are so many more important bottlenecks that this one doesn't make sense to prioritize, but it still seems like it should make sense for them at some point even if it doesn't fall into the top 100 bottlenecks for Cerebras-enabled coding agents).

Another kind of thing that one might not call ambitious, but that speaks to the kind of thing that's possible, are games that I've made. There are games I've thought about and wanted to make that I don't think are generally enjoyable enough that they make sense for a real audience, but that I've wanted to play. For example, ever since reading David Gerrold's Star Wolf books in the 90s, I've wanted to play a game that implements combat as described in the books, which is a sort of like submarine combat. At least among realistic war games, this genre is extremely niche because almost everybody finds naval combat boring, and submarine combat is a particularly boring subgenre of naval combat games, so this doesn't really make sense as a money-making game, but it's so easy to implement games that I had an agent implement the game so I could play it for an hour or two. I never would've spent 10-20 hours implementing a game so that I could play it for an hour or two, but I'd spend 5 minutes. I've also previously mentioned implementing a game with the same rules as Scout and Guards of Atlantis 2. I was never going to take the time to implement these games by hand just so I have a way to play with my friends on the occasions where we can't get together in-person, but I'm happy to have an LLM bash these things out. And, of course, for people who want to make games with a wider audience, there's a game renaissance going on right now due to coding agents. It's pretty amazing how many interesting and creative games are being made now that having programming skills and the time to put them to use is no longer a bottleneck for making games.

Data analysis is another thing where the productivity multiplier can be very high and I can do all sorts of things I never would've done. As I've mentioned in a number of my last posts, I have way too many of these projects to really be able to write them up, even when attempting to write very quickly and bash out posts in half an hour apiece.

When I've talked to people about their one-off tooling, there's a lot of fun stuff people have done. For example, here's something Peter Geoghegan mentioned a month or two back:

I had Fable implement a custom Neovim Lua function that formats code according to my very specific preferences. This is both something I don't want to maintain myself and inherently a Rube Goldberg device. Theoretically I could accomplish the same outcome in a principled way by patching clang-format, but my requirements are so exact that I think that approach would never be satisfactory.

We use a tool call pgindent, which is our fork of bsd_indent. You can approximate the same formatting rules using clang-format, but that isn't good enough. If I commit something that isn't perfectly formatted/indented according to pgindent, I get a CI failure that I'm expected to fix quickly -- something I'd really prefer to avoid ...

Practically speaking, getting slick, clang-format-style formatting that avoids nag emails about misindented code requires a total architectural mess (I also don't want to spend the time developing a principled approach, but that's really a separate issue). The function allows me to effortlessly format a given block of code from Neovim, similar to the clang-format LSP integration. I'm being unreasonably fussy here, of course, but I find that LLMs allow me to be this exacting about tooling.

The function performs multiple passes: an initial formatting pass using clang-format/clangd, and a separate formatting pass using pgindent. I need it to do both because clang-format handles some cases correctly that pgindent misses. This is brittle because I only want to format the code within a range of lines selected via block visual mode (I don't want to run clang-format on code not added by my patch). This conflicts with pgindent's design; it can only format whole C files.

Figuring out which relevant subset of the temp whole file buffer needs to be copied back into my working buffer is nontrivial. The initial line range I selected doesn't directly map to the affected C AST elements. So the function uses tree-sitter to intelligently delineate the exact subset of the temp indented C code that needs to be copied back. The rules need to be fuzzy in exactly the right way for cases where my selection straddles the same block of code. There are a bunch of edge cases.

Another complicating factor is that pgindent relies on a typedef file generated with objdump to identify types; without that file, the formatting looks wonky. The formatting function dynamically generates any extra typedefs from clangd, for that one file, so I don't have to worry about a stale typedef file (I might have created a new struct seconds before running the formatting tool, I don't want to run objdump on the whole postgres binary each time, that'd blow up latency).

This appears to work perfectly. The latency is totally acceptable. I have only a vague understanding of how all this works, though. I don't even know Lua. This will probably continue to work, even as further changes are made to our fork of bsd_indent that somewhat alter how code is formatted, which happens from time to time.

I'm skeptical of the saaspocalypse. But I do think that LLMs are writing a lot of useful software that would have been insanely uneconomical to write any other way. There's an interesting small subset of software that'd be impossibly tedious for any human to maintain, relative to the value that it creates.

I also caught with Malis while writing this and found out about all sorts of fun stuff he's been doing. It's enough that writing it all up in detail could be its own post, but one fun thing is that, the last time I taked to him about pgrust verification, he mentioned using Kani to verify some parts of the code. He's since switched to Lean and has been using Lean to verify things that are too complex to do in Kani. This would be another topic for another post, but I wonder why people have generally settled on Lean for LLM-driven proofs (as opposed to, say, ACL2). I wonder how Lean would look in an updated version of this theorem prover comparison, or if someone were to run a theorem prover eval that's analogous to this language eval.

Of course, you can think of plenty of examples out of AI labs, such as a mid-sized team Anthropic building an internal replacement for GitHub as well as some other tooling in five months

A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months.

I think these kinds of examples are interesting and they point to where the industry will be in the not-so-far future, but what you can do with unlimited tokens, while relying on other infrastructure and tooling built with unlimited tokens doesn't tell you much about what you can accomplish today without unlimited funds. Projects like pgrust as well as projects that people I know do in their spare time (of which I've probably mentioned something like 1%—there are just a lot of these, like David Turner creating an skipper for podcasts that's "works for me" quality that works better than anything he could find, the spare-time projects Dennis Snell mentioned here, etc.) are more representative of what you can do today.

articles.title: The Goose Programming Language
articles.full_content:
The Goose Programming Language

A memory-safe systems language with no heap allocator, garbage collector, or lifetime annotations. In this repository's benchmarks, Goose runs faster than C++ and Rust while using less memory.

Tutorial · Reference · Specification · Packages · Samples · Benchmarks · Standard library

Goose has syntax familiar to C and Rust programmers, but there is no heap. Every dynamic value lives inline on a data stack managed by the compiler. Growth advances a pointer, and memory is freed when its scope ends. The language's type and lifetime rules make this memory model safe to use.

Why Goose

  • Faster than C++ and than safe Rust, while memory safe. Over sixteen benchmarks Goose runs at 3.3x the speed of idiomatic C++, 1.16x hand-optimized C++ and 1.12x the best safe Rust, on 1.9x, 1.3x and 1.2x less memory (results). These gains come from Goose's data layouts and memory model.
  • No allocator, no GC, no reference counting, no destructors. Memory is a handful of data stacks that the compiler assigns statically. Freeing a million-element structure is one store, however deeply it nests.
  • Growth preserves references. A reference into a growing array stays valid for as long as the array does. You keep typed references where C++ must 
    reserve
    and safe Rust uses 
    u32
    indices in the corresponding benchmarks.
  • Memory safe with zero annotations. No lifetime syntax, no aliasing or exclusivity rules, no 
    unsafe
    . The compiler infers what every reference is rooted in and rejects references that could outlive their owners.
  • Nested data stays inline. A string, an array of strings, a record with variable-size fields and an array of those records are each one contiguous block with no pointer in it. A record that is 160 bytes and an allocation in C++ is 29 bytes and none in Goose.
  • Enums that cost what they hold. Variable-mode ADTs give each value its own variant's size rather than the largest one's: 4x less memory and 2x the speed of a Rust 
    enum
    on the benchmark that exercises it.
  • Links narrower than pointers. A relative reference stores a typed, checked link as a 1, 2 or 4-byte offset. Structures built from them are position independent, so your data structure is already its file format: saving is a write, loading is a read plus a verification pass that rejects hostile bytes.
  • Everything is built in place, guaranteed. A value is constructed at its final destination through any depth of calls. 
    items.push(parse(line))
    writes the parsed record straight into the array, and returning a growable array by value costs nothing.
  • Returns across multiple calls. 
    return err from load
    returns from a function any number of frames up, statically checked, with no unwinder, no 
    Result
    type and no 
    ?
    on every call.
  • Threads that share nothing. A worker is compiled as a separate program with its own memory, and flat values cross typed queues as a 
    memcpy
    . Data races, locks, atomics and memory orderings do not exist in the language.
  • Generics and higher-order functions with no overhead. An untyped parameter is generic. Function values are compile-time entities, so 
    xs.filter() { it > 0 }
    compiles to the loop it looks like and builds its result straight into its destination.
  • Plain C in, plain C out. Goose compiles to one C file, so it runs wherever a C compiler does and calls C directly through 
    extern fn
    . The bundled TinyCC backend compiles and runs a program in-process, with no build step.

The tutorial walks through all of this by example, the reference covers the whole language topic by topic, the specification has the exact rules, and the benchmarks have the numbers, losses included.

Features

This section focuses on what distinguishes Goose. The tutorial explains these features in more detail, and the samples show them in thirty-one complete programs.

One memory model: stacks, and scope exit is the free

A program has the native call stack, static data and N data stacks, where the compiler works out N. A data stack is a large address-space reservation with a bump pointer, and there is no other memory. At most one resizable value is live per stack and it is always on top, so growth never moves anything and never checks a capacity. All of this is proved at compile time; the runtime tracks only the bump pointers.

      
for round in 3 {
    var scratch: u8[>..] = [];                        // grow-only: growth is a pointer bump
    for i in 100000 { scratch.push((i % 256) as! u8); }
    print("round ", round, ": ", scratch.len, " bytes");
}                                                     // the free: one store to the stack top

Nothing moves, so references survive growth

      
struct Item { id: i32, weight: f32 }

var items: Item[>..] = [];
let first .= items.push(Item { 1, 0.5 });             // a reference to element 0
for i: i32 in 2..1000001 { items.push(Item { i, 0.0 }); }
first.weight = 99.5;                                  // still valid, a million pushes later

    

push
returns a reference to the new element, so a program can link elements while building the array. A 
vector<T>
or 
Vec<T>
may reallocate and cannot provide this guarantee. Stable references account for several benchmark gains.

Safe references, no annotations

Every reference and slice has a static root: the variable that bounds its target's lifetime. A reference must not outlive the variable that owns its target or access that target through an incompatible type. The compiler infers roots and specializes functions for them, so no annotations are needed. There are no aliasing or exclusivity rules. When a lifetime check fails, the error names the reference's root and its destination:

      
fn longest(a: u8[:], b: u8[:]) -> u8[:] { if a.len >= b.len { a } else { b } }

var outer: u8[>..] = [];
var w = outer[..];
{
    var inner: u8[>..] = [];
    format(inner, "inner text");
    w = longest(outer, inner);     // error: storing a reference rooted at inner,
}                                  //        which does not outlive the destination (§9.2)

A slice 

T[:]
lets a function accept a range from any array kind without copying its elements. For example, 
split
returns slices into its input, and a dictionary keyed by 
u8[:]
stores views of strings rather than copies.

Nested data stays inline

There is no single array type. There is a family that differs only in what happens to the size, and every member is 

[metadata][elements...]
, inline and packed, never a pointer to an element block:

Spelling What it is 
T[k]
 fixed size, known at compile time
T[]
, 
T[varint]
 sized at construction, frozen after; a fixed or variable-width length
T[..k]
, 
T[..]
 capacity inline; grows and shrinks within it
T[>..]
 grow-only: the workhorse; references into it stay valid 
T[>..<]
 grow-shrink: stacks, queues, heaps

Strings are just 

u8
arrays: 
u8[>..]
is a builder, 
u8[]
a finished string stored inline in whatever holds it, 
u8[..16]
a small string inside a struct, 
u8[:]
a view. A struct may contain variable-size parts, and they sit inline in declaration order, so a record is a run of bytes with nothing indirect in it:

      
struct Item  { sku: u8[varint], qty: varint, cents: varint }
struct Order { id: varint, customer: u8[varint], items: Item[varint] }

var book: Order[>..] = [];
book.push(Order { id: 1001, customer: "alice",
                  items: [Item { sku: "SKU-441", qty: 2, cents: 1999 },
                          Item { sku: "SKU-7", qty: 1, cents: 500 }] });

That order is 29 bytes and 0 allocations. As C++ 

std::string
+ 
std::vector<Item>
it is 160 bytes and 1 allocation, and as Rust 
String
+ 
Vec<Item>
153 bytes and 4. A whole order book is one array that streams through the cache. The price is that an array of variable-size elements is sequential: you can iterate it but not index it (unless you keep a second array of references into it as an index).

Enums in two sizes

Algebraic data types are the only dynamic polymorphism: no inheritance, no vtables. Every ADT can be stored two ways, chosen at the point of use. Fixed mode (

Shape
) is a tag plus room for the largest payload, indexable and overwritable. Variable mode (
Shape..
) gives each value exactly its variant's size; the array becomes sequential and a value never changes variant, and in exchange you may take references into a payload:

      
enum Shape { Circle { r: f64 }, Rect { w: f64, h: f64 }, Dot }

var packed: Shape..[>..] = [];                 // 9, 17 and 1 bytes, not 17 each
packed.push(Shape.Circle { r: 1.0 });
packed.push(Shape.Rect { w: 2.0, h: 3.0 });
packed.push(Shape.Dot);
for s in packed {
    match s { Rect &r => { r.w += 1.0; }, _ => {} }   // edits the payload in place, inside the array
}

Case functions provide another way to dispatch on a variant: define one overload per variant. Calls dispatch on the tag through a jump table, and the compiler checks that the overloads cover every variant:

      
fn area(s: Shape.Circle) -> f64 { 3.14159 * s.r * s.r }
fn area(s: Shape.Rect) -> f64   { s.w * s.h }
fn area(s: Shape.Dot) -> f64    { 0.0 }

for s in packed { print(s, " area ", area(s)); }

Links narrower than pointers

A 

T&
is a machine address: eight bytes, never dangling. A relative reference is the same link stored as a narrow offset: 
T&<u32>
is measured from the field itself to a target in the same array, so the structure is position independent, and 
T&<u32 in pool>
from a named pool's base, so other arrays can link into the pool. 
T&<u32>?
uses offset 0 as null. Here is a binary search tree in one grow-only array, with 12-byte nodes:

      
struct Node { key: i32, left: Node&<u32>?, right: Node&<u32>? }   // 12 bytes, links included

fn insert(pool: Node[>..]&, key: i32) {
    if pool.len == 0 { pool.push(Node { key: key }); return; }
    var cur .= pool[0];                             // .= binds a reference; = would copy the node
    loop {
        if key == cur.key { return; }
        let next = if key < cur.key { cur.left } else { cur.right };
        if next { cur .= next; continue; }          // narrowed by `if`: next is a Node&
        if key < cur.key { cur.left .= pool.push(Node { key: key }); }
        else             { cur.right .= pool.push(Node { key: key }); }
        return;
    }
}

References are transparent (no 

*
, no 
->
), 
.=
binds or retargets one, and 
Node?
is a nullable reference that 
if
, 
guard
and 
assert
narrow. The insert is one push and one store, and the push cannot invalidate 
cur
. When lifetimes are not nested, a 
reusable
pool pairs a grow-only array with a hidden freelist: 
alloc_ref
reuses a slot or pushes, 
free
hands one back, and since nothing is ever actually freed, a stale slot reads a different value of the correct type rather than corrupting memory.

Your data is already a file format

      
var image: u8[>..] = tree.to_bytes();           // a framed byte image of the whole array
var loaded, ok = from_bytes<Node[>..]>(image);  // verified before it becomes a value
image[image.len - 3] = 200;                     // tamper with a link ...
var bad, bok = from_bytes<Node[>..]>(image);    // ... and it is false and an empty array

The tree's links are self-relative, so it means the same thing wherever it sits: saving is writing its bytes and loading is reading them back, with no serializer, no schema and no pointer fixups. 

from_bytes
checks the framing, every tag, every length and every link before the bytes become a value, so a corrupt or hostile file is a 
false
, never a wild reference.

Built in place, always

The copy-free construction guarantee (spec §4.3) says a constructed value is always built in its final home, propagated top-down through calls. A function returning a grow-only array by value writes its elements straight into the caller's variable, or into a field of the record being built inside another array, so out-parameters mostly do not appear.

      
words.push(str("word", i));                    // formatted straight into the new element
let evens = xs.filter() { it % 2 == 0 };       // built straight into `evens`: no temporary
book.push(Order { id: 1001, customer: "alice", items: parse_items("SKU-441:2:1999;SKU-7:1:500") });

Returning errors across calls

      
struct User { name: u8[..16], age: i32 }

fn load(text: u8[:]) -> User[>..], u8[] {
    var users: User[>..] = [];
    each_split(text, '\n') { users.push(parse_user(it)); };
    return users, "";
}

fn parse_user(line: u8[:]) -> User {              // returns a User: no Result, no error parameter
    let comma = find(line, ",");
    guard comma >= 0 else { return [], str("expected name,age: ", line) from load; }
    let age, ok = parse_int(line[comma + 1..]);
    guard ok else { return [], str("bad age: ", line) from load; }
    let name = trim(line[..comma]);
    return User { name: name, age: age as i32 };
}

    

return E from f
returns 
E
as the result of the innermost active call of 
f
, however many frames up, and every function in between keeps its plain signature. It is checked statically, so every call of 
parse_user
must lie inside a 
load
call and nothing is uncaught at runtime. It is a hidden discriminant checked per frame rather than an unwinder, and the message is built directly where 
load
's caller wants it. The parsers in the samples use it for every syntax error.

Generics and function blocks

      
fn twice(x) { x + x }                              // an untyped parameter is a generic one

fn each_pair<T, F>(xs: T[:]) {                     // F is a function value: a compile-time entity
    for i in 0..xs.len - 1 { F(xs[i], xs[i + 1]); }
}

fn first_gap(xs: i64[:]) -> i64 {
    each_pair(xs) { a, b => if b - a > 1 { return a; } };   // returns from first_gap, not each_pair
    return -1;
}

let evens = xs.filter() { it % 2 == 0 };
let total = fold(xs, 0) { acc, x => acc + x };
sort(xs) { a, b => a > b };

Everything is monomorphized. Type arguments are inferred from argument types; parameters absent from those types can be supplied explicitly. Function values are passed as generic parameters: every call is direct and inlinable, they cannot escape, and there are no closure objects or function pointers, so a higher-order function compiles to exactly the loop it looks like. A block may 

return
from its lexically enclosing function, and nested functions see the enclosing function's locals.

Threads that share nothing

      
thread_fn worker() {                                // a separate program with its own memory
    loop {
        let job = qget<Job>();                      // blocks on the typed queue for Job
        guard job.n >= 0 else { break; }            // -1 means stop
        qput(Result { n: job.n, digits: count_digits(job.n) });
    }
}

for i in n { ids.push(thread_spawn(worker)); }

There is no shared mutable memory. A 

thread_fn
and everything it calls is compiled as its own program with its own data stacks and its own copies of the globals. Values cross through typed queues, one per type, and must be flat, with no references at any depth. That is cheap because a flat Goose value is contiguous: a job or a result carries real data, pixels included, and crossing is a 
memcpy
.

A failed check or 

abort
in a worker started with 
thread_spawn_contained
ends only that worker. Its message goes to whoever waits for it, not to stderr, so a supervisor can log it and start another:

      
var why: u8[>..] = [];
while !thread_wait(thread_spawn_contained(serve, attempt), why) {
    log(why);                                       // "assert failed (serve.goose:12)"
    why.clear();
    attempt++;
}

The first 

thread_wait(id, msg)
for a worker takes the message; a caller that doesn't ask for it loses it.

Plain C in, plain C out

      
extern fn hypot(x: f64, y: f64) -> f64;             // straight from libm
extern fn crc32_bytes(s: const u8[:]) -> u32;       // a slice crosses as { data, len }
extern fn stats_of(xs: i32[:], out: Stats&);        // a struct filled through a pointer

An 

extern fn
binds a Goose signature to a C symbol. The 
math
and 
os
modules use this interface. Only types with supported C representations may cross the boundary; unsupported signatures are rejected at the declaration. The compiler emits one C file for the whole program. The bundled TinyCC backend can compile and run that C inside the Goose compiler's process.

Where the speed comes from

Much of the speed comes from the memory model: no heap allocation or per-object teardown, contiguous data, narrow links, and enums sized for the variant they contain. Every index is bounds-checked, and the compiler removes checks it can prove unnecessary. An 

assert
on a slice length often lets a kernel eliminate its remaining checks and vectorize. 
--bce-lines
reports the checks that remain. 
checkfree fn
rejects a kernel if any bounds check survives; index types let graph edges retain validation done during construction. Benchmark measurements use whole-process wall-clock time, including teardown.

Geometric mean over 16 benchmarks vs idiomatic C++ vs hand-optimized C++ vs best safe Rust
speed, MSVC backend 3.51x 1.24x 1.13x
speed, clang backend 3.54x 1.26x 1.19x
peak memory 1.95x less 1.32x less 1.25x less

The summary explains the gains and losses; results.md has every measurement, and design.md explains what the suite tests.

What it costs you

  • You think about where data lives: who owns this, and how long does its scope last. Usually the answer is "the function that builds it", and that is free; when it is not, it is a 
    reusable
    pool.
  • Recursive functions cannot keep growable data across a recursive call; scratch ends before the call, and what outlives it is passed in as a pool.
  • Arrays of variable-size elements iterate but do not index (short of an index of references kept beside them), a fixed-mode enum cannot be pointed into, and a variable-mode one cannot be overwritten. You choose per container.
  • No escaping closures, no function pointers, no dynamic dispatch beyond ADT tags, and whole-program compilation only.
  • A slot handed back to a 
    reusable
    pool and still named reads whatever its next owner put there: a logic bug, never memory corruption.

Tutorial §18 is the full list.

Install a release

Prebuilt compilers for Windows (x64), Linux (x64) and macOS (Apple silicon and Intel) are on the releases page, with the graphics, audio, ui and physics packages compiled in. Unpack one anywhere and put its directory on PATH: the compiler finds the standard library, TinyCC's runtime and the packages beside itself, and keeps what it builds under 

~/.goose
(
GOOSE_HOME
). The archive also holds these docs, the samples and the VS Code extension.

Running a program in-process (

goose file.goose
) needs nothing else on Windows. On Linux it needs the C library's headers (
libc6-dev
, or 
glibc-devel
); on macOS, the SDK of the Xcode command line tools (
xcode-select --install
). 
goose build
also needs a C compiler: Visual Studio 2022 or later, or clang, on Windows; gcc or clang elsewhere. The Linux compiler needs glibc 2.35 or later (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12), the macOS one macOS 13.3 or later. macOS keeps a downloaded archive's files from running until 
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine
is run on the unpacked directory.

Build and run

You need CMake 3.27 or later, a C++20 compiler (MSVC, clang or gcc) and Python 3 for the test and sample runners. TinyCC, which the in-process backend is built from, is part of the tree. The graphics, audio, ui and physics modules are packages in repositories of their own (goose_gfx and goose_physics; 

docs/design/packages.md
): 
-DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all
fetches them at the pinned tags (git, at configure time) and compiles them into the compiler, so their programs run with nothing else installed. Without it the compiler builds alone, and a program importing one of them has it built into 
~/.goose
the first time, which needs git, cmake and a C compiler.

      
git clone https://github.com/aardappel/goose
cd goose
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DGOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS=all
cmake --build build --config Release

    

GOOSE_BUILTIN_LIBS
can also name some of the packages (
physics
, or 
gfx
, which carries 
audio
and 
ui
too). On Linux, SDL needs the X11 or Wayland development packages (
third_party/SDL/docs/README-linux.md
); without them the build leaves the 
gfx
module out and says what to install.

The runner scripts prefer 

build/Release
, then 
build/RelWithDebInfo
, then 
build
, then 
build/Debug
. Pass 
--exe
to select a specific compiler; use an explicit Debug executable when testing with compiler assertions enabled. The compiler is 
build/goose
(
build/Release/goose.exe
with the Visual Studio generator), and it finds the standard library in the source tree it was built from. On Windows 10 version 1903 and later, its embedded manifest selects a UTF-8 process code page so compiler paths do not depend on the system locale. Earlier Windows versions retain their legacy code page. Generated native executables retain their own process settings.

Run a program straight from source, in-process (

goose run
says the same explicitly, and 
goose check
only typechecks):

Or build an executable, which lands beside the source (

-o
puts it elsewhere). The compiler finds a C compiler on the machine (
goose toolchain
says which: MSVC or clang on Windows, cc, gcc or clang elsewhere; 
--cc
chooses) and links the generated C with the runtime and whatever native modules the program uses, graphics included. Programs that use threads need this route, since TinyCC cannot place thread-local storage.

      
build/goose build samples/01_tour.goose && samples/01_tour
build/goose build samples/27_gfx_cube.goose && samples/27_gfx_cube

    

--debug
turns on the overflow, range and tag checks in the generated C, each abort naming its source line (and an overflow or a cast the values involved), and builds the C with debug information; 
--dry-run
prints the commands a build would run, for a build system of your own; 
-v
prints them as they run. Intermediates go under 
~/.goose
(
GOOSE_HOME
), the runtime object compiled once per C compiler. Useful flags of both forms: 
-O0
/
-O1
/
-O2
set the inlining level (
-O2
by default), 
--bce-lines
reports the bounds checks kept per line, and 
-DGS_DEBUG=1
is what 
--debug
defines. Every resizable value lives on a data stack of 2 GB of reserved address space, committed as it is used: 
--stack-reserve 16G
changes that for a program, 
--stacks
reports how many data stacks the program and each of its workers can take and the cap that puts on 
hardware_threads()
, and 
-DGS_STACK_STATS=1
makes a program report its actual use as it ends.

A program with C of its own names it in a sidecar beside the source, 

foo.build
beside 
foo.goose
: 
c_sources = ["impl.c"];
, with 
c_include
, 
c_defines
, 
c_libs
and 
_windows
, 
_linux
or 
_macos
variants of each for one platform's part. Both forms build it: 
goose build
links it in, and 
goose run
builds it into a library the in-process run loads, so an 
extern fn
reaches it either way. A library does the same with a sidecar beside its entry (or names the static library target of its own CMake project, 
cmake_target = "x";
, which the compiler builds through cmake), and a program takes a library with 
import name from "source";
in its root file: a directory (
"./lib"
), or a git repository at a tag or commit (
"owner/repo@v1"
on GitHub, 
"host/owner/repo@ref"
), fetched into 
~/.goose
and built there once per C compiler (
docs/design/packages.md
).

Underneath, 

goose -o tour.c tour.goose
writes the C, which holds the program and the part of the runtime that inlines into it; the rest of the runtime (the OS layer, data stack reservation, threads, printing) is one more C file, which 
goose --emit-runtime goose_runtime.c
writes, to be compiled once and linked with every program (
cc -O2 tour.c goose_runtime.o -o tour -lm -pthread
; on Windows 
cl /O2 tour.c goose_runtime.obj
). Build the runtime with the compiler and flags the programs use; it takes no 
-D
of its own, and a program from another version of the compiler fails to link against it. 
--standalone
writes a C file that holds the whole runtime instead, and builds on its own. A program using 
audio
, 
gfx
, 
physics
or 
ui
also links that module's layer, which 
goose --audio-link msvc|cc
, 
--gfx-link
, 
--physics-link
and 
--ui-link
name in a response file (
cc cube.c goose_runtime.o -o cube @$(goose --gfx-link cc)
, a ui program's before the gfx one it draws through). 
goose build --dry-run
prints all of this for the program at hand.

A program using 

audio
plays procedural mono/stereo PCM through SDL3 without opening a graphics window. See the audio reference.

The test suite and the samples run on Windows, macOS and Linux:

For editing, the VS Code extension gives syntax highlighting, the compiler's language server (

goose lsp
: errors as you type, hover, go to definition, completion, rename, symbols) and one-key runs through the JIT:

Other editors can run 

goose lsp
themselves; editors has the configuration for Neovim, Helix and Emacs.

Documentation

  • Documentation index: the map of everything below, and the root of the documentation site built from these files (how).
  • Tutorial: the friendly introduction, by example. Read this first.
  • Language reference: every feature, topic by topic, with a compiling example for each: the whole language, written to be read.
  • Language specification: the exact rules, when you want to know why something did not compile.
  • Samples: thirty-one complete programs in reading order, from a tour of the language to a JSON parser, a threaded Mandelbrot, a file tree built from two pools, a spinning cube on the GPU, thousands of boxes raining into a heap and a to-do list in windows of widgets.
  • Standard library: fourteen modules, all readable Goose under 
    stdlib/
    , including 
    gfx
    , graphics on SDL3's GPU API (how it is built), 
    physics
    , rigid body physics on Box3D (how it is built), and 
    ui
    , fonts, text rendering and game HUDs, windows and widgets on Nuklear, drawn through gfx (how it is built).
  • Building programs and using packages: 
    goose build
    , libraries from git repositories or directories, a program's own C, and how to make a package of your own.
  • Benchmarks: the numbers, with the full results and the design behind them.
  • Implementation notes: how the compiler works, pass by pass, and how it is tested.

Status

Goose is new. What exists today is a whole-program compiler of about thirty thousand lines of C++, the specification, the standard library, the samples, and a test suite that CI runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with an extra sanitizer job. Deliberately out of scope for now: moves for resizable values, more than one resizable per struct, labeled 

break
, namespace privacy, and more OS/library access. Open items are tracked in the specification's Appendix B.

License

Goose is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0.

Authors

Wouter van Oortmerssen: Language Design, Compiler Design, Coding standards. home page, twitter.

Claude Fable: Compiler implementation, Benchmarking, Sample & Doc writing.

History & Use of AI

This repo was produced almost entirely with AI, from a human language design. I had designed Goose several years ago, and had started to implement it, but running a game startup (which is built on another programming language of mine, Lobster) there was no time to finish it. Which was sad, because I knew Goose could do things other languages can't, and it should exist.

I had not expected AI to help with this until Fable came out. I thought it might be capable enough to do a good job. I made it essentially clone the style and structure of my other recent compiler (Lobster), which is why if you look at the code, it looks rather similar to that. My initial design had left lots of things unspecified, and lots of back and forth with Fable made me decide on all of those, and it is now a better language for it.

It is also an experiment in using AI to implement a new language, rather than reproduce an existing one.

You may wonder why I had it work in C++, if clearly I could have used any language, like Rust, or my own Lobster, or.. Goose itself (that may still happen). With Fable, it was my observation that it is almost equally capable in any language, and the strong guardrails of Rust or other languages are not as pressing as they once were. Since the compiler emits C, you likely already need to have a C/C++ compiler around, so sticking inside one ecosystem would seem to simplify deployment and adoption. I've also integrated libtcc and who knows what other C libraries in the future. And, like I said, to have the compiler code mimic my existing Lobster compiler seemed fun, at least I can read it like it is my own.

articles.title: Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell, blast radius affects many HTTP libs and apps
articles.full_content:
TL;DR

⚠️ Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 21st NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. On Thursday, Python disclosed that Python packages were vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 as well.

On Friday, October 23rd, it has become known that this CVE affects other major languages and service applications using HTTP, where patches are not yet fully available.

Check if you are decoding Brotli as a dependency within your libraries. Stay on guard for wider announcements and be ready to upgrade as soon as possible. If there is no patch available for a library or application that may be affected, we recommend disabling Brotli decoding until patches become available.

Update 4:12PM PT: Patches are available for libbrotli, Python, C++, NodeJS, bun, Envoy and more coming. Apache and Nginx do not decode brotli by default.

Update 4:15 PM PT: OpenAI shares that they discovered this vulnerability in February. While the root cause issue was fixed in the Brotli source code at the time, it wasn’t known that it gave rise to a security vulnerability. OpenAI's advisories here.
‍

What is Brotli?

Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

What is CVE-2026-111497?

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library.

A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code.

OpenAI found this in February reported it as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses.

The root cause was fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't recognized as a security issue at the time and no release shipped with the fix until now. That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update.

‍You’re exposed if any environment has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x installed, since HTTP clients such as requests, httpx, and aiohttp load these packages automatically when they’re present. Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild any container images that bundle them. As of October 23, advisory databases don’t map the CVE to either PyPI package, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won’t flag vulnerable versions yet.

‍You can see what we’ve tracked here in Aikido Intel. 

As for unaffected software, Apache’s standard 

mod_brotli
does not decode Brotli

How to patch HTTP2Shell CVE-2026-111497

For CVE-2026-111497, update the affected runtime or Brotli library:

  • Node.js: upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, or a newer supported release in the corresponding release line.
  • Native Brotli / libbrotli: upgrade to 1.2.1 or later. For older release lines, use patched 1.0.10 or 1.1.1.
  • Python packages: upgrade Brotli to 1.2.1 or later and brotlicffi to 1.2.1.0 or later, wherever installed.
  • curl / libcurl: update its Brotli dependency to 1.2.1, a patched older release, or the vendor’s security-fixed package. Bundled or statically linked copies require an updated application build.
  • Bun: upgrade to 1.4.4 or later. Rebuild compiled executables that bundle Bun.
  • Envoy: upgrade to 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, or 1.37.8, or a newer release in a supported branch. 1.36.12 also includes the fix, but the 1.36 branch is unsupported.
  • Istio: the fix is included in 1.29.9, 1.30.6, and 1.31.2. Use a newer supported release in the corresponding line; the 1.29 branch is end of life.
  • Operating-system packages: install the vendor’s security update. Vendors may backport the fix without changing the upstream version number.
  • Other HTTP servers, reverse proxies, API gateways, and HTTP clients: update the affected runtime or Brotli library they use. Where Brotli is bundled into the product, install the product vendor’s release that explicitly addresses this CVE. For managed services, confirm remediation with the provider.

Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components.

‍

What to do if you can't upgrade yet

These workarounds reduce exposure while you prepare the upgrade:

  • Python applications: where Brotli support is optional, uninstall both Brotli and brotlicffi from affected environments. Remove dependency extras such as httpx[brotli] and any other requirements that would reinstall them, then regenerate dependency locks and rebuild/restart workloads. HTTPX, Requests, and urllib3 retain gzip and deflate support without these optional packages. However, a server that sends Brotli anyway may produce an unreadable response or an application error; automatic fallback is not guaranteed.
    • Uninstalling both Python packages and restarting workloads removes the decoding paths provided by those packages for incoming and outgoing data. It does not remove separate Brotli decoders bundled into other runtimes, libraries, or products.
  • Incoming HTTP requests: reject requests whose Content-Encoding includes br at the reverse proxy, load balancer, or application middleware, before any vulnerable decoder processes the body. Match br case-insensitively, including within lists of encodings. 
  • Outbound HTTP requests: remove br from Accept-Encoding. Also disable Brotli response decoding or reject responses whose Content-Encoding includes br before decoding begins. Ensure this check occurs before automatic body processing; checking after the client has downloaded and decoded the response is too late.

Changing Accept-Encoding alone is insufficient: a malicious server can send a Brotli response regardless of what the client advertises, and urllib3 selects its decoder from the response’s Content-Encoding header.

Keep these controls in place until affected components are patched and verified. Review coverage as vendors confirm additional affected components or attack paths.

How Aikido helps with CVE-2026-111497

Aikido flags vulnerable versions of Brotli and brotlicffi in your repositories, container images, and dependencies, including when they arrive as transitive dependencies. Your dashboard shows which services still run a vulnerable version, so you can upgrade the ones that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies first. 

Once you've upgraded, Aikido checks if the finding is gone.

The timeline

Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 22nd NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. Users were exposed if their app or a library decompresses bad Brotli data (e.g. the built-in fetch(), body-parser).

The next day, Python released a security update that patches the same flaw; Python packages were also vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497. Brotli flaw may affect even more languages and service applications, given how widely integrated the library is downstream. It turns out OpenAI had found this back in February.

Techincal details of CVE-2026-111497

The flaw sits in

 DecodeBlockTypeAndLength()
, which handles block switches, the points where a Brotli stream changes which Huffman tree it uses. In vulnerable versions the function returns a plain boolean, and BROTLI_FALSE can mean either "this stream is malformed" or "I need more input." Callers can't tell the two apart, and on the fast path the decoder discards the return value entirely.

A crafted stream can declare a single block type and then exhaust that block's length, which forces a switch that can't succeed. The decoder then either reports that it needs more input for a stream that's complete, or keeps decoding with the block state it already had. That second path leads to the out-of-bounds write.

The upstream fix, google/brotli commit 0ed4268, makes the function return an error code and adds a new error, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH (-17). Decoding now stops on a format error on both the safe and fast paths. OSM diffed the Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 source distributions and found that 1.2.1 differs only in the version bump and the decoder changes from that commit.

‍

‍

Brotli vulnerabilities in Python libraries (CVE-2026-111497)

The Brotli flaw behind Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497)  affects Python. Two PyPI packages, Brotli and brotlicffi, compile the same vulnerable Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles. An official advisory was posted on GitHub. Brotli has 82.8 million downloads per month.

You're affected if any Python environment you run has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier, or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x, installed. Popular HTTP clients such as requests and httpx load these packages automatically when they're present. Some packages automatically install Brotli as a dependency such as Scrapy, while others require explicit mention of it. An attacker can reach the vulnerable decoder by sending a malicious Brotli response to a request your app makes, or by sending your app a request body compressed with Brotli. That means an app can be exposed without importing Brotli anywhere in its own code. It’s a popular transitive dependency, so check your systems.

To fix it, upgrade to the patched releases:

  • Brotli -> 1.2.1
  • brotlicffi -> 1.2.1.0

The release notes for both fixed versions don't mention the CVE. As of October 23, advisory databases don't map it to either PyPI package yet, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won't flag these versions.

Who is affected by CVE-2026-111497 in Python?

You’re affected if any of your Python environments have one of these packages installed:

Your code doesn’t have to import either package. These HTTP clients advertise Accept-Encoding: br and decode Brotli responses automatically:

  • urllib3 (and therefore requests) when Brotli or brotlicffi is installed
  • httpx with the brotli extra
  • aiohttp when Brotli is installed
  • Scrapy, and anything built on the clients above

Attacker data can reach the decoder through two routes:

  • Outbound requests. Your app fetches a Brotli response from a server an attacker controls, such as through a webhook delivery, URL preview, crawler or “fetch this URL” feature.
  • Inbound requests. Your framework or middleware decodes a request body sent with Content-Encoding: br, which is the Python equivalent of the Express 5 case in Node.js.

How to fix CVE-2026-111497 in Python

The fix is a package upgrade, and it takes four steps:

  • Upgrade whichever package you have installed with pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1" or pip install -U "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0". If you use a lockfile with Poetry, uv, or pip-tools, update the constraint and regenerate the lockfile.
  • Rebuild your container images and any wheels that bundle either package. An image built on a vulnerable version stays vulnerable until you rebuild it.
  • Check every environment you run, including laptops, CI runners, servers and containers. Many projects pull in Brotli through an HTTP client extra, so look at your full resolved dependency tree.
  • Rely on a manual check for now. pip-audit, Dependabot and Safety won't report this until the advisory databases map the CVE to the PyPI packages.

If your Python Brotli bindings came from a Linux distribution package instead of PyPI, the fix comes through your distribution, so check its security advisory as well.

What is the Python Brotli vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497)?

Python Brotli vulnerability refers to CVE-2026-111497, the Brotli decoder flaw known as Node2Shell, as it affects Python packages on PyPI. The CVE record pairs CWE-252 (unchecked return value) with CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write).

How serious is CVE-2026-111497 for Python, and is it being exploited?

The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, and Node.js rates it high severity. OSM built Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 with AddressSanitizer and ran a crafted stream through both. Version 1.2.0 consumed all of the roughly 23 MB stream and kept reporting that it needed more input, whether the stream arrived in one piece or in chunks as small as one byte. Version 1.2.1 rejected the stream with error -17 every time.

OSM didn't pursue memory corruption or code execution in the Python extension. The decoder code is the same code that researchers exploited against an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build, as Imperva and others reported. For Node.js, The Hacker News reported no exploitation in the wild as of October 22.

Treat it as urgent anyway. The bug is a memory-safety flaw in a component that handles untrusted network input, and the fix is a routine version bump. Services that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies should go first.

How to check if your Python app is exposed

  • Check installed versions with pip show Brotli brotlicffi in each environment, and with docker run --rm <image> pip show Brotli brotlicffi for each container image.
  • Find what pulls the packages in. Run pipdeptree -r -p Brotli to see which dependencies require it, and search your lockfiles with grep -i brotli poetry.lock uv.lock requirements*.txt.
  • List the outbound HTTP calls that go to servers you don't control, and any endpoints that decode Content-Encoding: br request bodies.
  • Upgrade the services that match step 3 first, then the rest.

If you're reproducing the bug from Python, brotli.decompress() raises a generic brotli.error: decoder failed for any error, so you can't see which error code fired. A Decompressor() fed the crafted stream incrementally will never finish on 1.2.0.

FAQ

‍Which versions fix CVE-2026-111497 in Python?

Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0, along with any newer releases.

Do I need to import Brotli in my code to be affected?

An installed package is enough. urllib3, requests, httpx and aiohttp use Brotli or brotlicffi automatically when either is present and decode Brotli responses from any server your app calls.

Will pip-audit or Dependabot flag this?

Not yet. As of October 23, the CVE record, OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database don't list either PyPI package. OSM is submitting PYSEC entries and a PyPI package mapping for the GitHub advisory so that tooling picks this up.

Is there a workaround?

Uninstalling Brotli and brotlicffi removes the vulnerable decoder, and HTTP clients fall back to gzip and deflate. Rejecting Brotli-encoded requests at the edge reduces inbound exposure, but it doesn't protect against Brotli responses your app fetches.
